title: Collisions, and why MD5 and SHA-1 are dead
summary: The birthday bound, how real collisions broke MD5 and SHA-1, and how to pick a hash today.

steps.title: Collisions must exist; finding them must be hard
body: A 256-bit digest has 2^256 possible values, but there are infinitely many inputs, so collisions **exist** (pigeonhole). The promise is only that nobody can *find* one.

The **birthday bound** says how hard that is for a perfect hash: with an n-bit digest you expect a collision after about **2^(n/2)** random tries, not 2^n. (In a room of just 23 people, two probably share a birthday.)
| 64 bits | 2^32, a few seconds on a laptop |
| 256 bits (SHA-256) | 2^128, beyond any computer that will ever exist |
This is why digests and tags are never truncated to a handful of bytes for security.

steps.prompt: An ID scheme uses the first 8 bytes (64 bits) of SHA-256 as a unique document id. Roughly how many documents until two collide by chance?
steps.explain: Birthday bound: 2^(64/2) = 2^32. Fine for a small archive, a real risk at internet scale, and trivial for an attacker who *wants* a collision.

steps.title: Find a collision yourself
prompt: Truncate SHA-256 to its **first 2 bytes** (16 bits) and the birthday bound says a collision comes after a few hundred tries. Find one.

Hash the messages `m0`, `m1`, `m2`, ... (UTF-8) in order, remember each 2-byte prefix (as lowercase hex) in a `Dictionary<string, string>`, and stop at the **first** message whose prefix you have already seen. Print:
hints: Loop `for (int i = 0; ; i++)` and build `"m" + i`.
`SHA256.HashData(bytes)[..2]` is the first two bytes; `TryGetValue` tells you if the prefix was seen.

steps.title: How MD5 and SHA-1 fell
body: Real hash functions are not perfect, and cryptanalysts find shortcuts far below the birthday bound:

- **MD5** (128-bit): practical collisions in 2004; by 2008 researchers forged a trusted CA certificate with one, and in 2012 the *Flame* malware used an MD5 collision to fake a Microsoft code-signing certificate. Collisions now take seconds.

- **SHA-1** (160-bit): Google's *SHAttered* (2017) produced two different PDFs with the same SHA-1. In 2020 a **chosen-prefix** collision (attacker picks both starting documents) cost about $45,000 of GPU time. Browsers and CAs had already stopped trusting SHA-1 signatures.
Collisions break anything that signs or trusts a *digest*: get a victim to sign the harmless document, and the signature is valid for its evil twin.
Today: **SHA-256**, **SHA-384**, **SHA-512** (the SHA-2 family) or **SHA-3**. MD5 and SHA-1 are acceptable only where no attacker is involved, such as spotting accidental corruption in a cache.

steps.prompt: Is this use of a hash acceptable today?
items: SHA-256 to fingerprint release files that are also signed
SHA-1 in a new document-signing system
SHA-512 as the hash inside an HMAC
MD5 to dedupe a local cache with no untrusted input
MD5 to check a download against a value on the same website
steps.explain: The test is whether an attacker can benefit from a collision. A download check on the same site is doubly broken: MD5 collides, and whoever can swap the file can swap the digest.

steps.prompt: An attacker gets a CA to sign a harmless-looking certificate request, then presents a different, malicious certificate that carries the same signature. Which property did the hash fail?
options: Collision resistance: the attacker prepared both inputs
steps.explain: This is exactly the 2008 rogue-CA attack on MD5. The attacker controlled both documents, so they only needed a collision, the weakest property.
128, 160, 256 and 512 bits. Size alone is not safety: SHA-1's 160 bits did not save it once shortcuts were found.

steps.title: A hash with its name attached
prompt: Systems that store digests should record *which* hash made them, so they can migrate later (this is **crypto agility**, covered in module 6).

Write `string Fingerprint(string algorithm, byte[] data)` returning `"<algorithm>:<lowercase hex>"` for `sha256`, `sha384` and `sha512`. For `md5` or `sha1` (or anything else) throw `NotSupportedException`.

Then write `bool Matches(string fingerprint, byte[] data)` that splits on the first `:`, recomputes with the named algorithm and compares. It returns `false` (not an exception) when the algorithm is not supported.
solution: _ => throw new NotSupportedException($"{algorithm} is not allowed"),
template: Dojo.Eq("sha384 has 96 hex characters", 7 + 96, Fingerprint("sha384", dojoAbc).Length);
Dojo.Eq("sha512 has 128 hex characters", 7 + 128, Fingerprint("sha512", dojoAbc).Length);
Dojo.Check("Matches accepts the right data", Matches(Fingerprint("sha512", dojoAbc), dojoAbc), "returned false");
Dojo.Check("Matches rejects changed data", !Matches(Fingerprint("sha256", dojoAbc), "abd"u8.ToArray()), "returned true");
Dojo.Check("Matches rejects an md5 fingerprint", !Matches("md5:900150983cd24fb0d6963f7d28e17f72", dojoAbc), "accepted md5");
